value.overview: The Yellow-faced Grassquit is a small seed-eating songbird of the tanager family. Males are olive-green above with a black face and breast, bright yellow throat and eyebrow, and a yellow spot below the eye. Females and young birds are duller, with less distinct yellow markings. It is often seen in pairs or loose groups in grassy, weedy places, where it feeds actively on grass seeds and gives a thin, rapid, trilling song.
value.classification: The Yellow-faced Grassquit is a passerine in the tanager family, Thraupidae. Its scientific name is Tiaris olivaceus, and it is the only currently recognized species in the genus Tiaris.
value.identification: This grassquit is about 10–11 cm long and has a short, pointed, conical bill. The adult male has an olive-green back, dark wings, a black face and upper breast, and a striking yellow throat, eyebrow, and small spot below the eye. The lower underparts are grayish olive. Females are dull olive-green above and paler below, with faint or nearly absent yellow facial markings. Juveniles resemble females but are generally duller.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Mexico through Central America to northern South America and on several Caribbean islands. In Costa Rica it is a resident, generally common to abundant on both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes, including foothills, cultivated districts, the eastern Central Valley, and wetter highland areas. It is less typical of the dry northwestern lowlands. It favors open or semi-open habitats such as pastures, grassy roadsides, weedy fields, scrub, plantations, and gardens, usually from lowlands to roughly 1,900 m and locally higher.
value.migrationStatus: It is non-migratory and occurs year-round in Costa Rica. Local movements may occur as birds track grass seed supplies, rainfall, and suitable vegetation, but it is not a regular long-distance migrant.
value.breeding: Breeding can occur during much of the year in Costa Rica, with timing varying by rainfall, elevation, and local conditions. The female builds a roofed, roughly globular nest from grasses, weed stems, fibers, and other fine materials. A side entrance provides access. Nests are usually concealed in grass tussocks, weed clumps, low bushes, pastures, or grassy banks, commonly close to the ground but occasionally higher in shrubs. Clutches generally contain two or three pale, brown-speckled eggs.
value.dietFeeding: Grass seeds form the main part of the diet. The Yellow-faced Grassquit also eats other small seeds, berries, tender plant material, and some insects. It often feeds by perching on grass stems or hanging from seed heads to reach ripening grains, and it also picks fallen seeds from the ground. Insects may be gleaned from vegetation, especially when birds are feeding young.
value.behavior: This is an active, fairly social bird that is often found in pairs or loose groups, sometimes with other small seedeaters. It forages low in vegetation and frequently bends or clings to grass stems while feeding. Males may perch conspicuously on shrubs or grass tops to give a subdued, high-pitched trilling song. The species generally avoids dense woodland and is most easily detected in open countryside, gardens, and grassy edges.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not recognized as undergoing a major decline; the species remains widespread and locally common or abundant, including in Costa Rica.
